title: Quadratic expected message complexity for asynchronous crash consensus
formal: Does a randomized asynchronous binary consensus protocol exist with expected O(n²) messages against a strong adaptive adversary, tolerating every t<n/2 crash failures?
definitions: The n processes communicate by reliable asynchronous point-to-point messages and start with binary inputs. A crashed process takes no further steps. Every process that does not crash must eventually decide with probability one under fair scheduling; all decisions agree, and when all initial inputs are b every decision is b. A strong adversary observes past states, messages and revealed random outcomes and chooses subsequent process steps, message deliveries and crashes without seeing future coins. The bound counts all messages sent before protocol termination and must hold in expectation for every admissible adversary. It does not impose a bit bound on each message.

context_blocks.text: Randomization makes asynchronous agreement possible despite crash failures, but robustness to a strong scheduler affects its communication cost. A quadratic bound would reach a central efficiency frontier in the standard message-passing model.

Alistarh, Aspnes, King and Saia give nearly quadratic expected communication against a strong adversary. Their logarithmic overhead is not a proof of the exact quadratic target. This question concerns crash failures, separately from Byzantine behavior or private-channel security.

why: Determine the fundamental message cost of randomized agreement under adversarial asynchrony.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
